stem: Best guess: a business sells equipment it held 3 years at a gain smaller than the depreciation it took. What is the character of the gain?

choices.explanation: Correct. §1245 recaptures depreciation as ordinary income up to the gain.

explanation: §1245 recaptures depreciation as ordinary income up to the gain.

stem: Equipment cost $80,000; depreciation $30,000; sold for $95,000. What is the §1245 ordinary income and §1231 gain?
What is the purpose of the §1231 lookback rule?

choices.text: To extend the holding period of §1231 assets
To stop mixing ordinary losses and later capital gains
choices.explanation: Correct. Net §1231 gains are ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior 5 years.

choices.text: To recapture accelerated depreciation as ordinary
To allow capital losses to offset ordinary income
choices.explanation: That's not what the lookback does.

explanation: Net §1231 gains are ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior 5 years.

stem: An individual sells a rental building held 8 years: cost $500,000, straight-line depreciation $120,000, sold for $600,000. How much is unrecaptured §1250 gain?

choices.explanation: Correct. Gain = 600,000 − 380,000 = 220,000; the 120,000 attributable to straight-line depreciation is taxed at max 25%.

explanation: Gain = 600,000 − 380,000 = 220,000; the 120,000 attributable to straight-line depreciation is taxed at max 25%.

stem: A corporation sells the same building (cost $500,000, SL depreciation $120,000, price $600,000). What is the §291 ordinary income?
explanation: §291: 20% of the lesser of gain or straight-line depreciation.

stem: A business sells a machine held 8 months at a $5,000 loss. What is the character?

choices.explanation: Requires a holding period over 1 year.
Business property isn't a capital asset.
Correct. Business property held 1 year or less produces ordinary gain or loss.

explanation: Business property held 1 year or less produces ordinary gain or loss.

stem: A taxpayer has §1231 gains of $30,000 and §1231 losses of $(45,000) in 2025. What is the result?

choices.explanation: The capital loss limit doesn't apply.
Correct. Net §1231 loss is fully ordinary.

explanation: Net §1231 loss is fully ordinary.

stem: Which asset is §1231 property?

choices.explanation: Personal-use property is a capital asset.
Investment stock is a capital asset.
Correct. Depreciable or real property used in a business and held more than 1 year.

explanation: Depreciable or real property used in a business and held more than 1 year.

stem: Equipment that cost $60,000 was fully expensed under §179 and later sold for $25,000. What is the result?

choices.explanation: It was sold at a gain.
Correct. Basis is 0; gain 25,000 is less than the 60,000 deducted → all §1245 ordinary.

explanation: Basis is 0; gain 25,000 is less than the 60,000 deducted → all §1245 ordinary.

stem: In 2025, a taxpayer has a net §1231 gain of $20,000. In 2021 she had a net §1231 loss of $(12,000) and in 2023 a net §1231 gain of $5,000. How much of the 2025 gain is ordinary?
explanation: Nonrecaptured net §1231 losses = 12,000 − 5,000 = 7,000.

stem: A machine (cost $100,000; depreciation $40,000) is sold for $50,000. What is the result?

choices.explanation: Business property isn't a capital asset.
Correct. Loss = 50,000 − 60,000 = (10,000), a §1231 loss (ordinary if net §1231 is a loss).

choices.text: No loss is allowed on the sale

explanation: Loss = 50,000 − 60,000 = (10,000), a §1231 loss (ordinary if net §1231 is a loss).

stem: Why might an individual prefer to sell depreciable real property rather than equipment with the same gain and depreciation?

choices.text: Gains on equipment sales are tax-free to individuals
choices.explanation: Equipment gains are ordinary up to depreciation.

choices.text: Real property has no depreciation recapture of any kind
choices.explanation: Unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at up to 25%.

choices.text: Straight-line real property gain is capped at 25%
choices.explanation: Correct. §1245 recapture is ordinary (up to 37%); unrecaptured §1250 gain is capped at 25%.

choices.text: Real property gains are all taxed as ordinary income

explanation: §1245 recapture is ordinary (up to 37%); unrecaptured §1250 gain is capped at 25%.

stem: A §197 intangible (customer list) purchased for $150,000 with $50,000 of amortization is sold for $170,000. What is the character of the $70,000 gain?
explanation: Amortizable §197 intangibles are §1245 property.

stem: A disposition schedule shows equipment (cost $100,000; accumulated depreciation $70,000) sold for $90,000, and reports a $60,000 §1231 gain. What is the correct character of the gain?

choices.explanation: Depreciation recapture comes first for personal property.
Recapture is limited to the gain realized.
Correct. Gain is 90,000 − 30,000 = 60,000, all recaptured because it is less than the 70,000 of depreciation taken.
No §1231 gain remains when the gain is less than the depreciation taken.

explanation: §1245 recapture is the lesser of the gain or the depreciation taken; only gain above the depreciation is §1231 gain.

stem: A profitable business in the 21% bracket expects to be subject to much higher effective rates in 3 years. It buys equipment eligible for 100% bonus. What should it consider?

choices.text: Always take 100% bonus to get the deduction now
choices.explanation: Timing of deductions has value, but the rate matters.

choices.text: Deducting nothing now or later on the equipment
choices.explanation: Depreciation can't be forgone like that.

choices.text: Electing out, so depreciation falls in high-rate years
choices.explanation: Correct. Deferring deductions can increase their value when future rates are higher — compare the present value of the tax saved.

choices.text: Treating the equipment as inventory held for sale
choices.explanation: Equipment used in the business isn't inventory.

explanation: Deferring deductions can increase their value when future rates are higher — compare the present value of the tax saved.

stem: Equipment (cost $100,000; depreciation $60,000) is sold for $90,000: $10,000 down and a note for the rest. How much gain is recognized in the year of sale?

choices.explanation: Correct. All of the gain is §1245 recapture, recognized immediately.
Recapture isn't limited to cash received.
The installment method doesn't defer recapture.

explanation: §453(i): depreciation recapture is recognized in the year of sale even on an installment sale. Gain $50,000 ≤ depreciation $60,000, so it's all recapture.

stem: A business has a $10,000 casualty gain and a $25,000 casualty loss on business property held over a year. How is the net result treated?
explanation: Casualty gains and losses on long-term business property are netted first; a net loss is ordinary and doesn't go into the main §1231 netting.

stem: A machine used in a business for 3 years is sold at an $8,000 loss. With no other §1231 items, how is the loss treated?

choices.explanation: Correct. A net §1231 loss is ordinary.

explanation: Depreciable business property held over a year is §1231 property; a net §1231 loss is ordinary. Recapture applies only to gains.

stem: A business sells equipment it held 8 months at a $5,000 gain. How is the gain characterized?

choices.explanation: Correct. Business assets need a holding period over 1 year for §1231.
§1231 requires a holding period over a year.
It isn't a capital asset or long-term.

explanation: Depreciable business property held one year or less produces ordinary gain or loss.

stem: A client with no prior §1231 losses will sell one asset at a $100,000 §1231 gain and another at a $100,000 §1231 loss over the next two years. Which order is better?

choices.text: The loss asset first, the gain asset next year
choices.explanation: The lookback turns the later gain ordinary.

choices.text: The gain asset first, the loss asset next year
choices.explanation: Correct. The loss year stays ordinary and the gain stays capital.
The lookback rule makes it matter.

explanation: A net §1231 loss is ordinary, but it causes later net §1231 gains within 5 years to be recaptured as ordinary. Recognizing gains first avoids that.

stem: A taxpayer expensed a car under §179 when business use was 80%. In Year 3 business use drops to 40%. What happens?

choices.explanation: Correct. Listed property must stay above 50%.

explanation: If listed property's business use falls to 50% or less, the excess of §179 and accelerated depreciation over ADS straight-line is recaptured.

stem: Equipment cost $50,000, has $30,000 of accumulated depreciation and is sold for $60,000. How is the $40,000 gain characterized?

choices.explanation: Correct. Recapture is limited to depreciation.

explanation: §1245 recapture is the lesser of gain or depreciation; gain above original cost is §1231 gain.

stem: A business has a $15,000 casualty gain and a $10,000 casualty loss on long-term business property. Where does the net $5,000 go?

choices.explanation: Correct. A net casualty gain enters §1231.

explanation: Casualty items are netted first; a net gain goes into the main §1231 netting, while a net loss is ordinary.
